metric: CPU time of the core (src/gcm.c and its envelope) relative to bare OpenSSL EVP AES-256-GCM of the same shape: the random seal and the open over the bare random seal and open, which draw a random nonce as the core's random seal does, and the deterministic seal over a bare deterministic seal with the same hand-rolled HMAC-SHA256 nonce derivation (spec 1.8)
gate: for each size, the seal and open ratios (the core over bare EVP) and the det ratio (the core's deterministic seal over a bare deterministic seal of the same shape) must be at most the matching ceiling; the core's deterministic seal over its random one is recorded, never gated
runner_cpu: to be recorded from the bench workflow
note: A ratio, never nanoseconds, so it is portable across runners. Each benchmark runs five times in a random order and the gate reads the median of the raw repetitions. The ceilings are per size because the core's fixed per-call cost is a larger share of a small message; sizes live in tests/bench/benchmark.cc (kSizes). Both sides of det pay the same two HMAC-SHA256 computations (one over the label, one over be64(len(A)) || A || plaintext) and the same AES-GCM, so det is like-for-like whatever the runner's CPU accelerates. The deterministic seal over the random one is not like-for-like — it compares a SHA-256-bound seal with an AES-bound one — and an O17 probe found it ranging from about 1.2 to 9.6 across sizes, because AES-GCM and SHA-256 scale differently across runner CPU and libcrypto, so it is recorded, not gated. Refresh recorded_ratios from three runs and set a ceiling to the worst observed value across them times 1.2, rounded up to one decimal, never above its placeholder, only when it holds across the runs and both libcryptos.
